introduction_markdown:
Multiple choice paper (0780 Physics 1, June 2020, Advanced Level, one and a half hours). Answer ALL 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D; mark only one answer for each question (if you mark more than one you score zero). Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. Calculators and Formulae booklets are allowed.

**Constants used in the answers** (the paper itself prints no data sheet): speed of sound in air $340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (question 11, a question left open); no other constant is needed.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**Section I (thirty five questions), Questions 1-35.** Direction: Each of the thirty five questions or incomplete statements in this section is followed by four suggested answers. Select the best answer in each case.

**Section II (ten questions), Multiple Selection, Questions 36-45.** Directions: For each group of questions below ONE or TWO of the responses given is/are correct. Choose: A - if 1 and 2 are correct; B - if 2 and 3 are correct; C - if 1 only is correct; D - if 3 only is correct. (Directions summarised: A = 1, 2 only; B = 2, 3 only; C = 1 only; D = 3 only.)

**Section III (five questions), Questions 46-50.** Direction: Each of the questions (46-50) has four sets of graphs A - D. Which of the graphs in each question best fits the relationship between x and y?

incertitudes: Le sujet est un scan sans couche texte, avec filigranes (gcerevision.com) ignorés. Le sujet n'imprime ni feuille de données ni valeur de g ; seule la question 11 (laissée ouverte) a besoin d'une constante (vitesse du son retenue : 340 m s^-1).

Questions 11, 19, 28, 34 et 42 : le sujet imprimé est défectueux (donnée manquante ou options sans bonne réponse unique). Elles sont ingérées comme questions OUVERTES (auto-évaluation), avec les options recopiées dans l'énoncé, l'analyse dans le corrigé et aucune lettre désignée comme correcte.

Question 11 (premier harmonique supérieur d'un tuyau fermé, 128 Hz) : la valeur exacte est 0,89 m (v = 340 m/s) ou 0,86 m (v = 330 m/s) ; aucune des options (0,72 m ; 0,52 m ; 52 nm ; 7,2 m) ne convient. L'énoncé parle aussi d'un tuyau « de piano ».

Question 19 (ampèremètre 5,00 mA lu comme 5,00 A) : la résistance de l'ampèremètre n'est pas donnée, donc la valeur du shunt (en parallèle) est indéterminée : 0,49 ohm suppose R_g = 490 ohm, 0,02 ohm suppose R_g = 20 ohm.
Question 28 (boucle dans un champ sortant décroissant) : les options B (« counter clockwise ») et C (« anticlockwise ») sont synonymes, la réponse correcte (sens anti-horaire) figure donc deux fois.

Question 34 (barre composite) : la température de la jonction n'est pas imprimée ; le rapport des conductivités vaut 3(100 - t)/t, soit 1:1 seulement si t = 75 degrés C. Aucune option ne peut être retenue.

Question 42 (première loi de Newton) : telle qu'imprimée, seule l'affirmation 2 est vraie (la 3 est fausse : une force résultante est nécessaire pour changer la vitesse) ; aucune option « 2 only » n'existe ; B (2 et 3) serait la réponse si la 3 visait « maintenir une vitesse constante ».

Question 40 (essieu de train) : les affirmations 1, 2 et 3 sont toutes acceptables en physique idéalisée (pas de courant permanent dans un essieu isolé), alors que le format n'offre que « 1 et 2 », « 2 et 3 », « 1 seule », « 3 seule ». Clé la plus probable : A (1 et 2).

Question 43 (condensateur plan) : l'affirmation 2 imprime C = 2E/V (le carré sur V semble perdu à l'impression : correct serait 2E/V^2, ce qui donnerait B) ; telle qu'imprimée elle est fausse et la clé est D (3 seule). L'affirmation 1 (QV^2) est fausse dans tous les cas.

QCM conservés avec une clé retenue mais discutable : question 14 (B retenue ; C « a dual property » est une reformulation vague), question 15 (C retenue : la légère baisse avec la feuille de papier indique des alpha, le retour au bruit de fond avec 1,0 cm d'aluminium exclut les gamma), question 38 (le nombre de protons n'est pas conservé en désintégration beta moins), question 41 (l'affirmation 1 est lue comme la conservation de l'énergie totale), question 46 (C retenue : seul graphe avec une portion droite entre deux courbures ; D, en S, est défendable ; le coude visible en C est un défaut de tracé), question 47 (B : force répulsive seule, décroissante ; C remonte légèrement à droite).

Défauts d'impression sans conséquence sur la clé : question 7, options C et D imprimées sans racine carrée (seule B a la dimension d'une vitesse) ; question 12, la figure 1 est un schéma à la main, les flèches T1, T2, T3 désignent les courbes de la plus basse à la plus haute ; question 25, « hysterisis » et « cross bands » (pour cross-links) recopiés tels quels ; question 31, « shown figure 6 » recopié tel quel ; question 44, « of the thermal conductivity » (mot en trop) recopié tel quel.

Section II : le scan imprime les affirmations 1), 2), 3) ; les directions A à D sont résumées dans le tableau « Directions Summarised » (A = 1, 2 only ; B = 2, 3 only ; C = 1 only ; D = 3 only), recopié dans enonce_intro_markdown. Section III : le sujet ne marque aucune lettre en gras (aucune clé imprimée n'a été utilisée).

Aucun point imprimé : toutes les questions ont le même poids (points laissés vides). Aucune clé officielle n'existe : tous les corrigés sont rédigés et recalculés (questions 6, 8, 18, 24, 27, 30, 31, 35, 45 vérifiées par script).

Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 40, 43. Question 40 : aucune option exacte (voir ci-dessus, clé visée A). Question 43 : l'affirmation 2 est vraisemblablement tronquée à l'impression (clé visée D telle qu'imprimée, B si C = 2E/V^2).

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following are both base units in the S.I. system of units?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The seven SI base units are the metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol) and candela (cd).

- **A:** ampere and metre are both base units.
- **B:** the coulomb is a derived unit ($1\ \mathrm{C}=1\ \mathrm{A\,s}$).
- **C:** the volt is derived ($\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-1}}$).
- **D:** the ohm is derived, although the kelvin is a base unit.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Select the sets of quantities that both have the same units
questions.corrige_markdown:
Compare the SI units of each pair.

- **A:** electrical resistivity $\rho=RA/l$ is in $\Omega\,\mathrm{m}$; thermal resistivity (the inverse of thermal conductivity, $\mathrm{m\,K\,W^{-1}}$) has different units.
- **B:** work function is an energy ($\mathrm{J}$) but the Planck constant is in $\mathrm{J\,s}$.
- **C:** pressure is force per unit area, $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{Pa}$; the Young modulus is stress over strain, and strain has no unit, so it is also in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{Pa}$. Same units.
- **D:** energy is in $\mathrm{J}$ while the rate of change of momentum is a force, in $\mathrm{N}$ ($\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$).

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Energy and rate of change of momentum

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle oscillates with undamped simple harmonic motion. Which one of the following statements about the **acceleration** of the oscillating particle is true?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In SHM, $a=-\omega^2x$ and the speed is $v=\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2}$.

- **A:** the speed is greatest at the equilibrium position, where $x=0$, so $a=0$ is least there. True.
- **B:** the acceleration points towards equilibrium, so it is opposite to the velocity only while the particle moves away from the centre; it is not always opposite.
- **C:** $a=-\omega^2x=-4\pi^2f^2x$ is proportional to $f^2$, not to $f$.
- **D:** the potential energy $\tfrac12 m\omega^2x^2$ increases with $|x|$, and so does $|a|$; they increase together.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: It is least when the speed is greatest.
It is always in the opposite direction to its velocity
It is proportional to the frequency.
It decreases as the potential energy increases

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following waves **CANNOT** be polarised?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Only transverse waves can be polarised, because only they have oscillations perpendicular to the direction of travel that can be restricted to one plane.

- Radio waves and ultraviolet radiation are electromagnetic waves, which are transverse.
- A horizontal string plucked vertically carries a transverse wave (already plane polarised in the vertical plane).
- **Ultrasonic waves** are sound waves, which are longitudinal in a fluid, so they cannot be polarised.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: A horizontal string plucked vertically in the middle

questions.enonce_markdown: A typical fission reaction in a nuclear reactor is represented: $^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U}+{}^{1}_{0}n\rightarrow{}^{92}_{36}\mathrm{Kr}+{}^{141}_{56}\mathrm{Ba}+N\left({}^{1}_{0}n\right)$. The value of $N$ is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Conserve the nucleon number: $235+1=236=92+141+N\times1=233+N$, so $N=3$.

Check the charge: $92=36+56$, which balances because neutrons carry no charge.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The heating element of an electric kettle has a resistance of $30.0\ \Omega$. The kettle is connected to an a.c. power supply of root mean square voltage $230\ \mathrm{V}$. The peak value of the current is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The r.m.s. current is $I_{rms}=V_{rms}/R=230/30.0=7.67\ \mathrm{A}$.

The peak current is $I_0=\sqrt2\,I_{rms}=1.414\times7.67=10.8\ \mathrm{A}$.

The trap is **A** ($7.7\ \mathrm{A}$), the r.m.s. value, which is not the peak value.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An Earth satellite of mass $m$ revolves at a height $h$ from the surface of the Earth. If $R$ is the Earth's radius and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface of the Earth, then the velocity of the satellite is given by:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The gravitational force supplies the centripetal force at orbital radius $r=R+h$:

$$\frac{GMm}{(R+h)^2}=\frac{mv^2}{R+h}\ \Rightarrow\ v^2=\frac{GM}{R+h}.$$

At the surface $g=GM/R^2$, so $GM=gR^2$ and

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{gR^2}{R+h}}.$$

This is option B (options C and D have no square root and cannot have the dimensions of a velocity, and A has the wrong power of $R$).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A container is filled with a sample of an ideal gas at a pressure of 1.5 atm. The gas is compressed isothermally to one-fourth of its original volume. What is the new pressure of the gas in atmospheres?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Isothermal change of an ideal gas obeys Boyle's law, $pV=\text{constant}$:

$$p_2=p_1\frac{V_1}{V_2}=1.5\times4=6\ \mathrm{atm}.$$

The trap is **C** (4), which comes from adding instead of multiplying.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: It is observed that light of wavelength 430 nm just begins to emit photoelectrons from a surface. What is the quantum prediction if the wavelength of the incident light is changed to 440 nm?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Light of $430\ \mathrm{nm}$ only just reaches the threshold, so $430\ \mathrm{nm}$ is the **threshold wavelength**: photon energy $hc/\lambda_0=\phi$.

At $440\ \mathrm{nm}$ the wavelength is longer, so the frequency and the photon energy $E=hc/\lambda$ are lower than the work function: $E<\phi$. Each photon is too weak to free an electron, and in the quantum model intensity cannot compensate, because one electron absorbs one photon. No photoelectrons are emitted, so the photocurrent is zero.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: There will be a change in the photo current

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is an application of the Doppler shift?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Doppler shift is the change in observed frequency when a source and an observer are in relative motion. Radar speed guns send out a wave and measure the shift in the frequency reflected from a moving car.

- A, C: finding the frequency or wavelength of a tuning fork has nothing to do with relative motion.
- B: line emission spectra come from electron transitions.
- **D:** detecting cars moving at high speed on highways uses the Doppler shift.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Determining the frequency of a tuning fork
Determination of wavelength of sound produced by turning fork.
Detecting cars moving at high speed on highways.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The fundamental note produced by a closed pipe in a piano is 128 Hz. What is the wave length of its first overtone ?

*Options as printed:* A) 0.72 m   B) 0.52 m   C) 52 nm   D) 7.2 m
questions.corrige_markdown:
A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so only odd harmonics exist: $f_1,\ 3f_1,\ 5f_1,\dots$. The **first overtone** is the second note, the third harmonic:

$$f=3\times128=384\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$

With the speed of sound in air $v=340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (the paper prints no value):

$$\lambda=\frac{v}{f}=\frac{340}{384}=0.885\ \mathrm{m}\approx0.89\ \mathrm{m}.$$

(With $v=330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ the result is $0.86\ \mathrm{m}$.) None of the printed options matches: $0.72\ \mathrm{m}$ would need $v\approx276\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, which is not the speed of sound in air.

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The state of an ideal gas was changed three times at three different temperatures. Figure 1 represents three different isothermal curves. Which of the following is true about the temperature of the gas?

![fig-1](gce-al-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
On a $P$-$V$ diagram an isothermal is a curve $PV=nRT=\text{constant}$. The higher the temperature, the larger the product $PV$, so the curve lies **further from the origin**.

In Figure 1 the arrow for $T_1$ points to the curve closest to the axes, the arrow for $T_2$ to the middle curve and the arrow for $T_3$ to the outermost curve. Hence $T_1<T_2<T_3$.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A mass M is attached to a spring X, as shown in figure 2 (a). It is then displaced downwards and released so that it oscillates with a period T. If an identical spring is connected to it in series as shown in figure 2(b) and the same mass M is attached to it, what is the new period?

![fig-2](gce-al-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
For a mass on a spring $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$.

Two identical springs of constant $k$ in series each carry the same force $F$ and each extends by $F/k$, so the total extension is $2F/k$ and the combined constant is $k'=k/2$.

$$T'=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k/2}}=\sqrt2\times2\pi\sqrt{\frac mk}=T\sqrt2.$$

The trap is **A** or **D**, which treat the springs as if the period depended linearly on the number of springs.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Wave - particle duality with respect to electrons, means that :
questions.corrige_markdown:
Wave-particle duality means that a single entity shows both particle-like and wave-like behaviour.

- **B** states this exactly: electrons behave both as particles and as waves.
- A describes photons (quanta of energy), not electrons, and says nothing about waves.
- C ("a dual property") is only a vague restatement of the term, without saying which two properties.
- D is a piece of evidence for the wave nature only.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Electrons are tiny packages of energy that are charged
Electrons behave both as particles and as waves

questions.enonce_markdown: A radioactive source is placed 2.0 cm from a detector. The count rate decreases slightly if a sheet of paper is inserted between the source and the detector. It is reduced to the background radiation level if the sheet of paper is replaced by a 1.0 cm thick sheet of aluminium. What form (s) of radiation does this source emit?
questions.corrige_markdown:
- Alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper (and by a few cm of air); the **slight** drop in count rate with the paper shows that a small number of alpha particles are emitted (the source is only $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the detector).
- Beta particles pass through paper but are stopped by a few mm of aluminium.
- Gamma rays are only weakly absorbed, even by $1.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ of aluminium.

With $1.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ of aluminium the count falls to the background level, so no gamma is emitted. The source emits alpha and beta radiation only.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A gas molecule of mass m moving with velocity u collides at right angles with the side of a container and rebounds elastically. Which one of the following statements concerning the motion of the molecule is **NOT** correct?
questions.corrige_markdown:
For an elastic rebound at right angles the speed is unchanged and the velocity reverses.

- **A:** the speed is the same, so $\Delta E_k=0$. Correct.
- **B:** $\Delta p=mu-(-mu)=2mu$ in magnitude. Correct.
- **C:** Newton's third law: the two forces are equal in magnitude. Correct.
- **D:** the magnitude of the change in momentum is $2mu$, not zero. **This is not correct.**

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: The change in kinetic energy of the molecule is zero.
The magnitude of the change in momentum of the molecule is 2mu.
The force exerted by the molecule on the side of the container is equal to the force exerted by the container on the molecule.
The magnitude of the change in momentum of the molecule is zero.

questions.enonce_markdown: Interference fringes, produced by monochromatic light, are viewed on a screen placed a distance D from a double slit system with slit separation s. The distance between the centres of two adjacent fringes (the fringe separation) is w. If both s and D are doubled, what will be the new fringe separation?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The fringe separation is $w=\dfrac{\lambda D}{s}$.

With $D\to2D$ and $s\to2s$: $w'=\dfrac{\lambda(2D)}{2s}=w$. The separation is unchanged.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A $1\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor is charged using a constant current of $10\ \mu\mathrm{A}$ for $20\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the energy finally stored by the capacitor?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Charge stored: $Q=It=10\times10^{-6}\times20=2.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{C}$.

Energy: $E=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}=\dfrac{(2.0\times10^{-4})^2}{2\times1\times10^{-6}}=\dfrac{4.0\times10^{-8}}{2\times10^{-6}}=2\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{J}$.

The trap is **C**, which forgets the factor $\tfrac12$ ($QV$ or $Q^2/C$).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
An ammeter of full scale deflection $5.00\ \mathrm{mA}$ is being used to read a current of size $5.00\ \mathrm{A}$. This can be achieved by:

*Options as printed:* A) connecting it series with a resistance of $980.00\ \Omega$   B) connecting it in parallel with resistance of $49.95\ \Omega$   C) connecting it in parallel with a resistance of $0.49\ \Omega$   D) connecting it in parallel with a resistance of $0.02\ \Omega$
questions.corrige_markdown:
To extend the range of an ammeter a low-resistance **shunt** is connected **in parallel** with it (a series resistor would only reduce the current and extends a voltmeter range, so A is wrong).

At full scale the meter carries $I_g=5.00\ \mathrm{mA}$ and the shunt carries $I-I_g=5.00-0.005=4.995\ \mathrm{A}$, with the same potential difference across both:

$$R_s=\frac{I_g R_g}{I-I_g}=\frac{0.005}{4.995}R_g\approx\frac{R_g}{999}.$$

The resistance $R_g$ of the meter is **not given**, so the value of the shunt cannot be found: $0.49\ \Omega$ would need $R_g\approx490\ \Omega$ and $0.02\ \Omega$ would need $R_g\approx20\ \Omega$. A parallel shunt of $49.95\ \Omega$ would need $R_g\approx5\times10^{4}\ \Omega$, which is far too large for an ammeter. The correct method is a small parallel resistance; the numerical option cannot be chosen without $R_g$.

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: A ${}^{232}_{90}\mathrm{Th}$ nucleus decays by first emitting an alpha particle. It later decays by emitting two beta ($\beta^-$) particles. The resultant nucleus is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Alpha emission: ${}^{232}_{90}\mathrm{Th}\to{}^{228}_{88}\mathrm{Ra}+{}^{4}_{2}\alpha$ (A drops by 4, Z by 2).

Each $\beta^-$ emission raises Z by 1 and leaves A unchanged: Z goes from 88 to 90, A stays at 228.

The resultant nucleus is ${}^{228}_{90}X$ (an isotope of thorium). Option C is the nucleus after the alpha emission only.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
As the angle $\theta$ is increased, the coefficient of friction between the bottom surface of the block and the surface of the incline in figure 3 will:

![fig-3](gce-al-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The coefficient of friction $\mu$ is a property of the two surfaces in contact (their materials and roughness). It does not depend on the angle of the incline, so it **remains the same**.

What changes is the balance of forces: the component of the weight down the slope $mg\sin\theta$ increases while the maximum friction $\mu mg\cos\theta$ decreases. Once $\tan\theta>\mu$ the block slips down the plane.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: decrease and the object will not slip down the plane;
increase and the object may slip down the plane;
remain the same but the object may slip downwards;
decrease and the object will slip downwards.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following statements is correct according to Newton's first law of motion?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Newton's first law: a body remains at rest or moves with constant velocity in a straight line unless acted on by a resultant (net) force.

- A: contradicts the law (no friction means no halt).
- B: an object at rest acted upon by balanced forces does not move; only a net force makes it move.
- C: no force means a straight line, not a parabola.
- **D:** an object at rest remains at rest unless acted upon by a net force. Correct.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: an object in motion eventually comes to a halt;
if an object at rest is acted upon by a force, it must move.
an object in motion moves in a parabolic trajectory unless acted upon by a net force.
an object at rest remains at rest unless acted upon by a net force.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The value of X for which the galvanometer in figure 4 shows a null deflection is:

![fig-4](gce-al-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The circuit is a Wheatstone bridge: $X$ and $6\ \Omega$ form the top branch, $4\ \Omega$ and $3\ \Omega$ the bottom branch, and the galvanometer joins the two mid-points.

Null deflection means the mid-points are at the same potential, so the ratios of the potential differences are equal:

$$\frac{X}{6}=\frac{4}{3}\ \Rightarrow\ X=\frac{4\times6}{3}=8\ \Omega.$$

The trap is **B** ($4\ \Omega$), which comes from inverting the ratio incorrectly.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An object weighs 100.0 N on the surface of the earth, the radius of which is R. If the object is raised through a distance R above the surface of the earth, it will weigh:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Weight follows the inverse square law, $W\propto1/r^2$ with $r$ measured from the centre of the Earth.

Raised by $R$ above the surface: $r=R+R=2R$, so

$$W=100.0\times\left(\frac{R}{2R}\right)^2=\frac{100.0}{4}=25.0\ \mathrm{N}.$$

The trap is **B** ($50.0\ \mathrm{N}$), which uses $1/r$ instead of $1/r^2$.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: For polymeric solids which of the following statements is true:
questions.corrige_markdown:
- **A:** false. Cross bonds (cross-links) between molecules are found in thermosetting polymers, not in thermoplastics, whose chains are held by weak forces and soften on heating.
- **B:** false. Car tyres are made from rubber (an elastomer, cross-linked and elastic), not from a thermoplastic.
- **C:** false. A small hysteresis loop is the property of rubber (nearly elastic); thermoplastics deform plastically and dissipate much energy, so their loop is large.
- **D:** true. Thermosetting polymers (for example bakelite) do not soften on heating, so they can be used for frying pan handles.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Thermoplastics have cross bands between their molecules
Thermoplastic polymers can be used in making car tyres
Thermoplastic polymers have a small hysterisis loop.
Thermosetting polymers can be used in making frying pan handles

questions.enonce_markdown: A hollow plastic ball and a solid metal ball all of the same external radius are both released from rest in a vacuum chamber. After falling for one minute, they will have the same;
questions.corrige_markdown:
In a vacuum there is no air resistance; both balls fall with the same acceleration $g$ whatever their mass, because the weight $mg$ is divided by the same mass $m$.

After the same time both have $v=gt$: the **same speed**.

Kinetic energy $\tfrac12mv^2$, inertia (mass) and change in momentum $mv$ all depend on the mass, which differs.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A physics student places an object 6.0 cm from a converging lens of focal length 9.0 cm. What is the magnitude of the magnification of the image produced?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The object is inside the focal length ($u=6.0\ \mathrm{cm}<f=9.0\ \mathrm{cm}$), so the image is virtual, upright and magnified.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A single circular loop of wire in the plane of the page is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B, directed out of the page as shown above. If the magnitude of the magnetic field is decreasing, then the induced current in the wire is:

![fig-5](gce-al-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

*Options as printed:* A) directed upwards out of the paper;   B) counter clockwise around the loop;   C) anticlockwise round the loop;   D) clockwise round the loop.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The flux out of the page through the loop is decreasing. By Lenz's law the induced current opposes this change, so it must produce a field **out of the page** inside the loop to try to keep the flux up.

By the right-hand grip rule, a current that produces a field out of the page through the loop flows **anticlockwise** as seen by the reader.

The correct answer is therefore "anticlockwise", but options B ("counter clockwise") and C ("anticlockwise") mean exactly the same thing, so the question has two equally correct options and no single letter can be designated.

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following statements describes an electric generator?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A generator converts mechanical energy to electrical energy by electromagnetic induction: a coil rotating in a magnetic field has an emf induced in it (Faraday's law), so a current flows in the circuit.

- A: describes nothing real (electric potential does not create a "temporal magnet").
- **B:** a coil of wire rotated through a strong magnetic field produces an electric current. Correct.
- C and D describe a motor (current in a field causes motion).

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Electric potential in a rotating coil of a wire creates a temporal magnet
A coil of wire is rotated through a strong magnetic field to produce an electric current
An electrical current causes a coil of wire to rotate in a magnetic field.
Forces from a permanent magnet allow a coil of wire to rotate

questions.enonce_markdown: A sample of an ideal gas is in a tank of constant volume. The sample gains heat energy and its temperature changes from $300\ \mathrm{K}$ to $900\ \mathrm{K}$. If $v_1$ is the average speed of the gas molecules before absorption of heat and $v_2$ the average speed after absorption of heat, what is the ratio $v_2/v_1$ ?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The mean kinetic energy per molecule is proportional to the absolute temperature, $\tfrac12m\langle c^2\rangle=\tfrac32kT$, so the r.m.s. (average) speed varies as $\sqrt T$:

$$\frac{v_2}{v_1}=\sqrt{\frac{T_2}{T_1}}=\sqrt{\frac{900}{300}}=\sqrt3.$$

The trap is **A** ($3/2$), which uses a ratio of temperatures wrongly.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A small vibrating object on the surface of a ripple tank produces waves of frequency $20\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and speed $60\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$. If the source S is moving to the right as shown figure 6, with a speed of $20\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$, what frequency would an observer at point C hear?

![fig-6](gce-al-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Point C is on the right of S, in front of the moving source, so the wavefronts are compressed there (the figure shows the circles crowded on the right).

The source moves towards a stationary observer:

$$f'=f\,\frac{v}{v-v_s}=20\times\frac{60}{60-20}=20\times1.5=30\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$

The trap is **B** ($13.3\ \mathrm{Hz}$), which uses $v/(v+v_s)$ for a source receding.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is correct?
questions.corrige_markdown:
- A: false. At the top of its path a ball thrown upwards is momentarily at rest, yet it has an acceleration of $g$ downwards.
- B: false. Velocity is a vector, so its direction can change (circular motion) while the speed is constant.
- C: false. A change in speed is a change in velocity, and this requires an acceleration.
- **D:** true. A body that is slowing down has an acceleration in a direction opposite to its velocity.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: It is NOT possible for a body to be at rest and yet have an acceleration;
A change in the velocity of an object implies a change in its speed;
It is possible for the speed of a body to change without the body accelerating.
A body can be accelerating in a direction opposite to that of its velocity.

questions.enonce_markdown: An impulse of 100 N s is applied to an object. If this same impulse is delivered over a longer time interval:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Impulse $=F\Delta t=\Delta p=100\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. The impulse is the change in momentum, and it is the same (100 N s) in both cases, so the momentum transferred does not change (options C and D are false).

If $\Delta t$ is longer, then $F=\Delta p/\Delta t$ is smaller: **the force involved will be decreased.**

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the force involved will be decreased;
the force involved will be increased;
the momentum transferred will be increased;
the momentum transferred will be decreased.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A composite rod is made of two materials X and Y and its two ends are maintained at $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ respectively, as shown in figure 7. If the composite rod is well lagged, what is the ratio of the conductivity of $y$ to that of $x$?

![fig-7](gce-al-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

*Options as printed:* A) 1:2   B) 2:1   C) 1:1   D) 1:4
questions.corrige_markdown:
In steady state the rate of heat flow $\dfrac{Q}{t}=\dfrac{kA\Delta\theta}{l}$ is the same in both parts (well lagged, same cross-section $A$). With $x=25.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ (at $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$), $y=75.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ (at $0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$) and a junction temperature $\theta$:

$$k_x\frac{100-\theta}{0.250}=k_y\frac{\theta-0}{0.750}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{k_y}{k_x}=\frac{3(100-\theta)}{\theta}.$$

The **temperature of the junction is not given** in the paper, so the ratio cannot be found: it is $1:1$ only if $\theta=75\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (uniform temperature gradient), and each other option needs a different $\theta$ ($1:2$ needs $\theta=85.7\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $2:1$ needs $\theta=60\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $1:4$ needs $\theta=92.3\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: A diffraction grating has 500 lines per millimetre and is illuminated normally by monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm. The total number of images seen on both sides of the normal including the central image is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Grating spacing: $d=\dfrac{1\times10^{-3}}{500}=2.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$.

The orders obey $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ with $\sin\theta\le1$, so

$$n_{max}<\frac{d}{\lambda}=\frac{2.0\times10^{-6}}{600\times10^{-9}}=3.33\ \Rightarrow\ n=0,\pm1,\pm2,\pm3.$$

Total number of images: $2\times3+1=7$.

The trap is **A** (5) or **B** (10): forgetting the central maximum or counting order 3.33 as 4.

**Answer: C.**

Translational equilibrium means zero acceleration, hence zero resultant force.

1. **True:** $\vec F_1+\vec F_2+\vec F_3=\vec 0$.
2. False: forces of $3\ \mathrm N$, $4\ \mathrm N$ and $5\ \mathrm N$ can be in equilibrium (they form a closed triangle of forces: $3^2+4^2=5^2$), so the magnitudes need not be equal; equal magnitudes (three $10\ \mathrm N$ forces at $120^\circ$) is only one special case.
3. False: concurrency of the lines of action is needed for rotational equilibrium (zero moment), not for translational equilibrium.

Only statement 1 is correct. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following experiments is an evidence that electrons exhibit wave properties?

1. The Electrons are negatively charged..
2. J.J Thomson's measurement of the charge to mass ratio of the electron.
3. Davisson and Germer's electron diffraction experiment
questions.corrige_markdown:
Diffraction is a wave property.

1. A statement about charge, not an experiment, and it shows particle properties.
2. Thomson's $e/m$ measurement treats the electron as a charged particle deflected by fields.
3. **Davisson and Germer** observed electrons diffracted by a nickel crystal with a maximum at the angle predicted by $\lambda=h/p$: evidence of wave properties.

Only 3 is correct. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following quantities are conserved in all nuclear reactions?

1. Electric charge
2. Number of nuclei
3. Number of protons
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. **Conserved:** the total charge is conserved in every reaction (as are the nucleon number and mass-energy).
2. Not conserved: in fission one nucleus gives two, in fusion two give one.
3. Not conserved: in $\beta^-$ decay a neutron changes into a proton, so the number of protons increases by one (it is the number of **nucleons** that is conserved, and the charge).

Only 1 is correct. **Answer: C.**

The string, its tension and its mass per unit length are unchanged, so the wave speed $v=\sqrt{T/\mu}$ is the same after reflection (1 false), and the frequency is fixed by the source and is not changed by reflection (2 false).

At the fixed end the string cannot move, so the reflected wave undergoes a phase change of $\pi$: the crest is reflected as a **trough** (3 true).

Only 3 is correct. **Answer: D.**

The horizontal axle (north-south) moves east through the vertical component $B_v$ of the Earth's field, so it cuts flux and an emf $\varepsilon=B_vlv$ appears between its ends.

1. **True:** $\varepsilon=B_vlv$ is proportional to $v$.
2. **True:** only the vertical component of the field is cut by a horizontal axle moving horizontally and perpendicular to it.
3. Statement 3 is also true in the usual idealisation: the axle is not part of a closed circuit (the rails are insulated from each other), so charge separates until the electric force balances the magnetic force and no steady current flows.

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are all acceptable in this idealisation, so no printed option is exactly right. The most likely intended answer is A (1 and 2), reading statement 3 as false because the wheels and rails could complete a circuit.

**Intended answer: A (1 and 2 are correct).**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A football is dropped from a height of 20 m above the ground. It rebounds to 3/4 of its original height. Which of the following statements is / are true ?

1) Energy is conserved during the impact.
2) Kinetic energy is constant during the impact.
3) The velocity with which it leaves the ground is 3/4 the velocity with which it hits the ground.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The ball falls from $20\ \mathrm m$ and rebounds to $15\ \mathrm m$.

1. **True:** total energy is always conserved; the mechanical energy lost ($25\%$ of the original) becomes thermal energy and sound in the ball and the ground.
2. False: the kinetic energy falls to zero at maximum compression and then rises again, and it is smaller after the impact than before.
3. False: $v=\sqrt{2gh}$, so $v_{up}/v_{down}=\sqrt{15/20}=\sqrt{0.75}=0.866$, not $0.75$.

Only 1 is correct. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following deductions is/are true from Newton's first law of motion?

1) The velocity of a body, in the absence of a resultant force, is always zero
2) A body is always reluctant to change its state of motion
3) A resultant force is NOT necessary to produce a change in velocity

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. False: with no resultant force the velocity is **constant** (possibly zero, possibly not).
2. **True:** this is inertia, the content of the first law.
3. False as printed: a resultant force **is** necessary to change the velocity (Newton's first and second laws). The statement is true only if it is read as "a resultant force is not necessary to produce (maintain) a constant velocity".

As printed only statement 2 is true, and no option offers "2 only". If statement 3 is read as "to maintain a constant velocity" the matching option would be B (2 and 3); this cannot be settled from the paper.

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A parallel plate capacitor connected across a battery of voltage V. if the charge on the plates of the capacitor is Q, then which of the following statements is / are correct?

1) The energy stored on the plates is $QV^2$;
2) If the energy stored in the capacitor is E, then its capacitance $C=\dfrac{2E}{V}$
3) The electric potential between the plates increases uniformly, from the negative to the positive plate.

*Options as printed:* A) 1 and 2 are correct   B) 2 and 3 are correct   C) 1 only is correct   D) 3 only is correct
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. False: the energy stored is $E=\tfrac12QV$ ($=\tfrac12CV^2=Q^2/2C$). $QV^2$ does not even have the dimensions of energy.
2. As printed, $C=2E/V$ is false: from $E=\tfrac12CV^2$ the capacitance is $C=\dfrac{2E}{V^2}$. (The statement is correct only if the square on $V$ was lost in printing.)
3. **True:** between the plates the field is uniform, $E=V/d$, so the potential changes linearly with distance, rising from the negative plate to the positive plate.

As printed only statement 3 is correct.

**Intended answer: D (3 only is correct).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
In the comparison of heat and electrical energy flowing along a well insulated conductor which of these is/are true?

1) The Pd across the ends of the conductor is analogous to the temperature difference between the ends of the conductor.
2) The electric current is analogous to the rate of flow of heat
3) The electrical resistance is analogous to the of thermal conductivity
questions.corrige_markdown:
The standard analogy is $I=\dfrac{V}{R}\leftrightarrow\dfrac{Q}{t}=\dfrac{\Delta\theta}{R_{th}}$ with $R_{th}=\dfrac{l}{kA}$.

1. **True:** potential difference corresponds to temperature difference.
2. **True:** current (charge per second) corresponds to the rate of flow of heat $Q/t$.
3. False: electrical resistance corresponds to the **thermal resistance** (inverse of conductance), and the electrical conductivity corresponds to the thermal conductivity.

Statements 1 and 2 are correct. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A car traveling at $60\ \mathrm{km\ per\ hour}$ passes a truck going at $30\ \mathrm{km\ per\ hour}$ that has four times the mass of the car. Which of the following is true?

1) The car and the truck have the same momentum and the same kinetic energy.
2) The truck has greater kinetic energy than the car.
3) The car has the same kinetic energy and half as much momentum as the truck.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let the car have mass $m$ and speed $v=60$ (km h$^{-1}$); the truck has mass $4m$ and speed $v/2=30$.

- Momentum: car $mv=60m$; truck $4m\times30=120m$. The truck has **twice** the momentum, so the car has half.
- Kinetic energy: car $\tfrac12m(60)^2=1800m$; truck $\tfrac12(4m)(30)^2=1800m$. They are **equal**.

1. False (momenta differ). 2. False (energies are equal). 3. **True.**

Only 3 is correct. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
$y$ = distance travelled by a cyclist that accelerates down a hill, then runs at a steady speed, before ascending the next hill, $x$ = time.

![fig-9](gce-al-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_9.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The distance travelled never decreases, and the gradient of a distance-time graph is the speed.

1. Accelerating down the hill: the gradient increases, so the curve bends upwards.
2. Steady speed: constant gradient, a straight section.
3. Ascending the next hill: the cyclist slows down, so the gradient decreases and the curve flattens.

Graphs A and B are wrong because in both the distance falls back to zero at the end (A) or after a plateau (B); a distance travelled cannot decrease, and a plateau would mean the cyclist has stopped. Graph C shows exactly the three stages: a curve bending upwards, a straight (steady) section, then a curve levelling off. Graph D has no straight section; it is an S-shaped curve with only one change of curvature.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
$y$ = the repulsive force between two molecules, $x$ = the distance between the molecules.

![fig-10](gce-al-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_10.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The repulsive force between molecules is strong at short range and falls off very rapidly (much faster than $1/x^2$) as the molecules move apart, approaching zero without ever becoming negative.

- A (straight line down) has a constant gradient, which is not the case.
- **B** shows a steep fall that flattens towards the $x$-axis: correct.
- C falls and then rises again, which would describe a force that changes character (the net force with the attraction included), not the repulsive force alone.
- D is constant.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
$y$ = the number of atoms of the stable isotope of lead produced from the decay of a fixed quantity of polonium, $x$ = time.

![fig-11](gce-al-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_11.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The polonium decays exponentially, $N=N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, and each decay leaves one atom of the stable lead isotope. The number of lead atoms is therefore

$$N_{Pb}=N_0-N=N_0\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right).$$

It starts at zero, grows quickly at first and then levels off at $N_0$ (all the polonium has decayed). This is graph **C**. Graph A is the decay of the polonium itself, B (a straight line) would need a constant decay rate, and D has the wrong shape (decreasing, positive at $t=0$).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
$y$ = the net force between two identical point charges moving away from each other, $x$ = the distance between the charges.

![fig-12](gce-al-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_12.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
By Coulomb's law $F=\dfrac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0x^2}\propto\dfrac1{x^2}$: the force is very large at small separation and falls towards zero (without reaching it) as $x$ increases. This is the decreasing curve of graph **A**.

B is a straight line, which would be a force falling linearly (and reaching zero), C and D show a force that increases with distance.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
$y$ = the mechanical energy of a simple pendulum swinging in a vacuum chamber, $x$ = time.

![fig-13](gce-al-physics-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_13.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
In a vacuum there is no air resistance, and an ideal pendulum has no friction at its pivot. Energy is exchanged between potential and kinetic during each swing, but the total mechanical energy is conserved, so it is **constant** with time. This is the horizontal line of graph D.

**Answer: D.**
